tips.title: The dates are boundaries, not walls
tips.body: A composer does not wake up in 1750 and start writing Classical music. The dates mark roughly where the **style** changed, and plenty of music sits across a line — Beethoven most famously of all. Use the dates to orient yourself, never to argue with your ears.

tips.title: Listen for the continuo first
tips.body: A **harpsichord or organ filling in chords under the bass line** is the single most reliable sign of the Baroque period. It disappears after about 1750, so hearing one dates an extract in a couple of seconds and hearing none rules the Baroque out.

tips.title: Count the lines, not the instruments
tips.body: Several independent melodies at once is **polyphony**, and it points backwards to the Baroque and earlier. One tune with support underneath is **homophony**, and it points forwards to the Classical period and after. That one test does most of the work.

tips.title: Dynamics tell you about the instruments
tips.body: Music that steps between loud and soft with nothing in between is **terraced**, and it usually means a harpsichord and an organ, which cannot get gradually louder. A real **crescendo** needs instruments that can, so it points to the Classical period onwards.

steps.title: The map, and what a period actually is
steps.body:
Western classical music is usually divided into periods. The dates below are the conventional ones, and they are **approximate on purpose**.

- **Medieval** — about 500 to 1400
- **Renaissance** — about 1400 to 1600
- **Baroque** — about 1600 to 1750
- **Classical** — about 1750 to 1820
- **Romantic** — about 1820 to 1900
- **Twentieth century** — about 1900 to 2000
- **Today** — from about 2000, usually called contemporary

A period is not a rule anybody obeyed. It is a label historians gave, afterwards, to a stretch of time in which music was mostly doing similar things. Composers did not change style overnight, and several of the most famous sit awkwardly across a boundary — **Beethoven** above all, whose early work is Classical and whose late work points into the Romantic period.

So the dates are for orienting yourself, never for arguing with your ears.

**One word causes endless trouble.** *Classical* with a small c means all Western art music — Baroque, Classical, Romantic, the lot. **Classical** with a capital C means one period of **70 years**, from 1750 to 1820. The specification's own vocabulary list makes exactly that distinction, so it can be examined.

Notice the lengths. The Baroque runs **150 years** and the Classical only **70**, so "Baroque style" covers far more ground than "Classical style" does.

boxes.title: Nobody announced them
boxes.body: The labels were applied afterwards by historians. No composer ever set out to write in a period.

boxes.title: Styles overlap
boxes.body: Old habits carried on while new ones started. A boundary is where the balance tipped, not where one stopped.

boxes.title: Composers straddle them
boxes.body: Beethoven begins Classical and ends pointing into the Romantic. He is the reason the 1820 line is drawn there.

boxes.title: Places differ
boxes.body: A style could be current in one city and old-fashioned in another, so any single date is a compromise.

steps.title: What each period sounds like
steps.body:
You will not be asked to recite dates. You will be played something and asked what it is. So learn each period by **what you can hear**.

**Medieval.** Mostly voices, often unaccompanied. **Plainchant** is a single line sung in unison — **monophonic**, however many singers there are. Modal rather than in a major or minor key. Sacred music for the church dominates what survives.

**Renaissance.** Several voices weaving independent lines — **polyphony** — with **imitation** everywhere: one voice states an idea and another takes it up while the first continues. Smooth, mostly stepwise, no strong beat driving it forward. Still largely vocal and largely sacred, though secular songs and dances grow.

**Baroque.** The **continuo** arrives and is the giveaway: a bass line with a chord-playing instrument, usually **harpsichord** or organ, filling in the harmony above it. Busy, ornamented, and built from **counterpoint** — independent lines woven together. **Terraced dynamics**: loud and soft in steps, because a harpsichord cannot get gradually louder. One mood per movement, held all the way through.

**Classical.** The continuo disappears. Texture becomes **melody and accompaniment** — one tune on top, support underneath. Balanced phrases, often in fours, that answer each other like sentences. Clear cadences. **Graded dynamics** — real crescendos — because the **piano** and a fuller orchestra can produce them. Lighter, clearer, more obviously tuneful than the Baroque.

**Romantic.** Everything gets bigger: a much larger orchestra, longer works, wider dynamic range, more **chromatic** harmony, more distant modulations. Music starts telling stories or painting pictures — **programme music** — and the emotional range of a single piece widens enormously.

**Twentieth century.** No single style at all. Some composers abandon keys altogether — **atonal** music; others use folk material, or machines, or chance. The only safe generalisation is that there is no longer one thing music is expected to be.

check.solution: A bass line plus a chord-playing instrument realising the harmony above it is the **continuo**, and it is the defining texture of Baroque ensemble music. It fades out after about 1750, so hearing one is strong evidence for the period and hearing none is evidence against it.

steps.title: The forces, and why they grew
steps.body:
The number of players tells you as much as the notes do.

- **Baroque**: around 20 players.
- **Classical**: around 40 players.
- **Romantic**: around 90 players.

So the Romantic orchestra is about **4.5 times** the size of the Baroque one. That is not fashion. Three things changed.

**Who was paying.** Baroque and much Classical music was written for a patron — a court, a church, an aristocrat — and played in their rooms to their guests. By the Romantic period music was increasingly performed in **public concert halls** to an audience that had bought tickets. A bigger room and a bigger audience need a bigger sound.

**What the instruments could do.** Valves gave brass instruments a full chromatic scale rather than a handful of notes, so they could carry melodies instead of just fanfares. Woodwind gained keys and became more agile and more reliably in tune. The piano replaced the harpsichord and kept growing louder.

**What composers wanted.** Once an orchestra could sustain, swell and change colour, composers wrote music that needed it.

**The sections of an orchestra**, in score order: **strings** (violins I and II, violas, cellos, double basses), **woodwind** (flutes, oboes, clarinets, bassoons), **brass** (horns, trumpets, trombones, tuba), **percussion**. The Baroque orchestra is strings plus continuo with a few extras; clarinets arrive in the Classical period; trombones, tuba and a large percussion section belong to the Romantic.

**And the keyboard.** The **harpsichord** plucks its strings with a quill, so pressing harder changes nothing and dynamics can only be terraced. The **piano** — short for *fortepiano*, meaning soft-loud — hits them with hammers, so touch controls volume directly. The instrument's name is the whole point of it.

check.prompt: Why can Baroque keyboard music not have a gradual crescendo?
options: The harpsichord plucks its strings, so touch cannot change the volume
Baroque composers had not yet thought of writing a crescendo
The rooms were too small for a crescendo to be heard
A crescendo would have been considered improper at the time
check.solution: A harpsichord plucks each string with a quill, so pressing a key harder does not make it louder. Dynamics can only change in **steps**, by switching manuals or stops, which is what **terraced dynamics** are. The piano solves it by striking the strings with hammers, which is why it is named for its ability to play soft and loud.

steps.title: The one change that matters most
steps.body:
If you remember a single thing from this topic, make it this.

> Baroque music is typically built from **counterpoint** — independent lines woven together. Classical music is typically built from **melody and accompaniment** — one tune on top, support underneath.

Almost everything else follows from that shift.

**Why the continuo disappeared.** A continuo exists to fill in harmony under contrapuntal lines. Once the music is a tune with an accompaniment, the accompaniment already *is* the harmony, and a harpsichord doubling it has nothing left to do.

**Why phrases became balanced.** In counterpoint each line has its own shape and they overlap, so the music does not fall into neat units. In melody and accompaniment the tune is in charge, and a tune naturally comes in phrases — often four bars answered by another four, like a question and an answer.

**Why the cadences became clearer.** Overlapping lines blur the ends of phrases; one tune with support does not, so the points of arrival are audible.

**Why the texture got lighter.** Four independent lines are four things to follow. One line plus support is one.

Test it on the two set works. Bach's **Brandenburg Concerto No. 5** (1721) is contrapuntal: the parts compete for your attention. Beethoven's ***Pathétique*** (1798) is a tune with an accompaniment, and you always know which is which. **77 years** separate them.

steps.title: Structures, period by period
steps.body:
Each period has forms it favours, so naming the structure often names the period.

**Baroque**

- **Binary** — two sections, usually both repeated. The first modulates from the tonic to the dominant or relative major; the second finds its way home.
- **Ternary** — three sections, A B A, with a contrasting middle.
- **Ritornello** — an orchestral idea returns between passages for the soloist. The backbone of the Baroque concerto.
- **Ground bass** — a short bass pattern repeating while everything above it changes. Purcell was a master of it, and *Music for a While* is a set work built this way.
- **Fugue** — a subject stated by one voice and taken up by each of the others in turn.
- **Dance suites** — a group of pieces in dance styles, such as a **gigue**, normally in compound time like 12/8.

**Classical**

- **Sonata form** — exposition, development, recapitulation. The large-scale form the period invented, and the one the *Pathétique* first movement uses.
- **Rondo** — a main section returning between contrasting episodes: A B A C A.
- **Minuet and trio** — a dance movement in three, with a contrasting trio and then the minuet again.
- **Theme and variations** — a theme stated plainly and then varied repeatedly.

**Romantic and after**

- **Programme music** — music that tells a story or paints a picture, often in one continuous movement.
- **Song cycles**, **character pieces** for piano, and symphonies that grow far longer than Classical ones.

Notice that **theme and variations** and the **ground bass** are the same idea from two directions: something fixed with something changing over it. One fixes the tune and varies it; the other fixes the bass and varies what sits above.

Sonata form is Classical; binary is two repeated sections; a fugue passes a subject from voice to voice.

steps.title: Who the music was for
steps.body:
Context earns marks in the exam only when it explains something you can hear. Here is the version that does.

**The church.** For centuries the church was the largest employer of musicians in Europe. That is why so much Medieval and Renaissance music that survives is sacred, why it is vocal, and why it is in Latin. Music written for a building with a long echo tends to move slowly and smoothly, because fast detail turns to mud.

**The patron.** In the Baroque and much of the Classical period a composer was employed by a court, a church or an aristocrat, and wrote what was wanted: music for a service, for a name day, for dinner, for a specific room and a specific group of players. Bach's Brandenburg Concertos are dedicated to a Margrave. The forces are modest because the rooms were.

**The public concert.** Through the Classical period and into the Romantic, concerts increasingly meant a hall, a ticket and strangers. A composer now writes for an audience they do not know, in a room far larger than a salon. The orchestra grows to fill it; the music grows longer and more dramatic to hold a crowd.

**The printing press and the domestic piano.** Once music could be printed cheaply and a middle-class household could own a piano, there was a market for music to be played at home. Short character pieces, songs and arrangements all follow from that.

> *Written in the Baroque period* earns almost nothing. *Written for a patron's own musicians in his own rooms, which is why the ensemble is about twenty players* earns, because the context explains something audible.

steps.title: Your turn: place three extracts
steps.body:
Three extracts, described. For each, name the period and give **two** reasons from the music. Two reasons matter: one is a guess, two is an argument.

**A.** Voices only, no instruments at all. One line of melody, sung in unison by all the singers, in Latin, with no regular beat you could tap and no sense of a major or minor key.

**B.** A string orchestra with a harpsichord filling in chords over the cello bass line. Three upper parts weave independent melodies. The music is loud for eight bars, then suddenly quiet for eight, with nothing in between. The whole movement keeps one mood.

**C.** A piano plays a singing tune in the right hand over broken chords in the left. Phrases come in fours and answer one another. The volume swells and fades continuously. There is no harpsichord anywhere.

Write your answers, then check them.

check.prompt: Extract C has a singing tune over broken chords, phrases in fours, and volume that swells and fades. Which period, and why?
options: Baroque: the broken chords are a continuo realising the harmony
Renaissance: the balanced phrases show imitation between the parts
Classical: melody and accompaniment, balanced phrases and graded dynamics
Romantic: any music with a swelling dynamic must be Romantic
check.solution: Three features agree. **Melody and accompaniment** rather than counterpoint, **balanced four-bar phrases** answering one another, and **graded dynamics**, which need an instrument that responds to touch. Broken chords in a left hand are an accompaniment, not a continuo; imitation needs parts taking up each other’s ideas; and a crescendo is possible from the Classical period onwards, so it does not on its own mean Romantic.

steps.title: Going deeper: a procedure for dating an extract
steps.body:
Under exam pressure you want a routine rather than an impression. This one works, and it works in order, because the early tests are the most reliable.

**1. Is there a continuo?** A chord-playing instrument filling in harmony over a bass line. If yes, Baroque, and you are nearly finished. If no, you have ruled the Baroque out.

**2. Count the melodic lines.** Several independent ones is **polyphony**, and points backwards: Renaissance or Baroque. One tune with support is **homophony**, and points forwards: Classical or later. Count lines, not players — ten violins in unison are one line.

**3. What do the dynamics do?** Steps with nothing between them are **terraced**, which means a harpsichord or organ, which means Baroque. Continuous swelling means instruments that respond to touch, so Classical onwards.

**4. What is the keyboard?** A harpsichord is bright, plucked and even in volume. A piano is warm, struck and can shade every note.

**5. How big is the ensemble, and what is in it?** Strings and continuo: Baroque. Strings, woodwind including clarinets, horns and trumpets: Classical. Trombones, tuba, a large percussion section: Romantic.

**6. How chromatic is it?** Baroque and Classical harmony is mostly diatonic with functional cadences. A lot of chromaticism and distant modulation suggests Romantic.

**7. Now check the date against your answer**, not the other way round.

And when you write it up, give **two reasons**. A period named with one reason reads as a guess; a period named with two independent reasons that agree reads as an argument, and that is the difference the mark scheme is looking at.

boxes.title: How many lines?
boxes.body: Several independent melodies is polyphony and points back. One tune with support points forward.

boxes.title: Terraced or graded?
boxes.body: Dynamics in steps mean a plucked keyboard. A real crescendo means Classical or later.

boxes.title: What is in the band?
boxes.body: Strings and continuo, or clarinets and horns, or trombones, tuba and a percussion section.

steps.title: What to carry forward
steps.body:
- The periods: **Medieval** 500–1400, **Renaissance** 1400–1600, **Baroque** 1600–1750, **Classical** 1750–1820, **Romantic** 1820–1900, **Twentieth century** 1900–2000. Approximate, and composers straddle them.
- **Classical** with a capital C is one period of **70 years**; **classical** with a small c is all Western art music.
- **Medieval**: monophonic plainchant, modal, sacred, Latin.
- **Renaissance**: polyphony with imitation, smooth and stepwise.
- **Baroque**: the **continuo**, counterpoint, **terraced dynamics**, ornamentation, one mood a movement.
- **Classical**: **melody and accompaniment**, balanced phrases, clear cadences, **graded dynamics**, the piano.
- **Romantic**: a large orchestra, chromatic harmony, programme music, a wide dynamic range.
- **Twentieth century**: no common practice; some music is **atonal**.
- The orchestra grew from about 20 players to about 90 — **4.5 times** — because the rooms, the audiences and the instruments all changed.
- The single biggest change is **counterpoint giving way to melody and accompaniment**, and the continuo, the phrasing, the cadences and the texture all follow from it.
- Your set works sit at the ends of Area of Study 1: Bach in 1721, Beethoven in 1798, **77 years apart**.
- Always give **two reasons** for a period.

questions.prompt: Forty singers perform a single line of plainchant in unison, unaccompanied. What is the texture?

Polyphonic
Monophonic
Heterophonic
questions.solution: **Monophonic**: only one note sounds at a time, that is, a single melodic line. Count the lines rather than the people — forty singers on the same tune are still one line. Homophony needs an accompaniment and polyphony needs independent melodies.

questions.solution: Baroque music is typically built from **independent lines woven together**; Classical music from **one tune with support underneath**. The disappearance of the continuo, the balanced phrasing and the clearer cadences all follow from that change.

questions.solution: **Ritornello** form, from the Italian for *little return*. It is the backbone of the Baroque concerto: the orchestral idea comes back between episodes for the soloist, often shortened and in different keys, so the listener always has something familiar to hold on to.

questions.prompt: Why can a harpsichord not play a gradual crescendo?

questions.solution: A harpsichord **plucks** each string with a quill, so how hard the key is pressed makes no difference to the volume. Dynamics can only change in steps. The piano **strikes** its strings with hammers, which is exactly why it can shade every note and why it is named after being able to play soft and loud.

questions.prompt: Put these periods of Western classical music into chronological order, earliest first.

questions.prompt: How many years longer is the Baroque period (1600 to 1750) than the Classical period (1750 to 1820)?

**What you hear:**

- A cello plays a continuous bass line in even quavers. A harpsichord plays chords above it, filling in the harmony, throughout.
- Two violins and a viola each play their own melody at the same time; none of them is obviously accompanying the others.
- Bars 1 to 8 are loud. Bars 9 to 16 are the same material, quiet, with nothing in between the two levels.
- The melodic line is heavily ornamented with trills and turns.
- The opening orchestral material returns at bar 33 and again at bar 57, each time in a different key, with passages for a solo flute in between.
- The mood does not change from the first bar to the last.

questions.solution:
**The period is Baroque**, about 1600 to 1750, and four independent features agree.

**The continuo.** A cello plays a continuous bass line while a harpsichord fills in the chords above it throughout. That combination is the **continuo**, and it is the single most reliable marker of the period: it is present in almost all Baroque ensemble music and essentially disappears after about 1750. On its own it would nearly settle the question.

**Texture.** Two violins and a viola each play their own melody at the same time and none is obviously accompanying the others, so the texture is **polyphonic** — independent lines woven together, which is also called **counterpoint**. That points backwards rather than forwards: Classical music is typically one tune with support underneath, and it would be obvious which part was which. It matters that the test is on the number of **lines** rather than of players; three instruments playing in unison would be one line and would prove nothing.

**Dynamics.** Eight bars loud and then the same material eight bars quiet, with nothing in between, is **terraced dynamics**. The reason is the instrument: a harpsichord **plucks** its strings with quills, so pressing a key harder does not make it louder, and a composer writing with one in the ensemble writes steps because steps are what is available. The absence of any marking on the page other than f and p says the same thing.

**Structure and style.** The opening orchestral material returning at bar 33 and again at bar 57, each time in a different key, with solo flute passages in between, is **ritornello** form — the backbone of the Baroque concerto. The heavy **ornamentation** of the melodic line with trills and turns is a Baroque habit, and so is holding **one mood** from the first bar to the last, where a Classical movement would set contrasting material against its opening.

questions.prompt:
An extract of instrumental music is played several times, with a skeleton score showing the right-hand piano part.

**On the page:** one sharp in the key signature; three crotchets in a bar; markings including cresc. and dim.

**What you hear:**

- A piano. The right hand plays a singing melody; the left hand plays broken chords underneath it throughout.
- The melody falls into four-bar phrases, each one answered by another four bars that finishes the idea.
- The volume swells gradually and then falls away again, several times.
- A clear cadence closes each pair of phrases; the first ends unfinished on chord V and the second closes on chord I.
- No harpsichord is heard at any point.
- After the opening section a contrasting middle section follows in a different key, and then the opening returns.

Identify the period this extract comes from, justify your answer from the music, and explain what the absence of a harpsichord tells you.
questions.solution:
**The period is Classical**, about 1750 to 1820.

**Texture.** The right hand plays a singing melody and the left hand plays broken chords underneath it throughout. That is **melody and accompaniment** — **homophony** — and it is the defining Classical texture. You always know which part is the tune, which is exactly what you cannot say about a Baroque contrapuntal movement, where the lines compete for attention.

**Phrasing and cadences.** The melody falls into **four-bar phrases**, each answered by another four that completes the idea, like a question and an answer. The first closes on **chord V**, unfinished — an **imperfect cadence** — and the second closes on **chord I**, finished: a **perfect cadence**. That pairing of an open answer with a closed one is a Classical habit, and it is only audible because the texture is clear enough for the phrase endings not to be blurred. In counterpoint the lines overlap and the joins are deliberately hidden.

**Dynamics.** The volume **swells gradually and falls away** several times, and the page carries cresc. and dim. markings. These are **graded dynamics**, and they require an instrument whose volume responds to touch. A harpsichord cannot do it, because it plucks; a **piano** can, because it strikes the strings with hammers — which is what its full name, *fortepiano*, meaning soft-loud, is about.

**What the missing harpsichord tells you.** Its absence is evidence, not an absence of evidence. A **continuo** is present in almost all Baroque ensemble music and gone after about 1750, so hearing none rules the Baroque out. There is also a musical reason for its disappearance: a continuo exists to supply harmony underneath independent contrapuntal lines, and once the music is a tune over an accompaniment the accompaniment already **is** the harmony, so there is nothing left for a harpsichord to fill in.

**Structure.** An opening section, a contrasting middle section in a different key, then the opening returning, is **ternary form** — A B A. It is not exclusively Classical, but it fits everything else here.

**Conclusion.** Homophonic texture, balanced phrases with paired cadences, graded dynamics and a piano rather than a harpsichord all point to the Classical period, and no feature in the extract points anywhere else.

questions.prompt: Compare Baroque and Classical instrumental music, referring to texture, the continuo, dynamics, phrasing and the instruments used. Explain how one change leads to the others.
questions.solution:
**The change that causes the others.** Baroque music is typically built from **counterpoint** — several independent lines woven together — and Classical music from **melody and accompaniment**, one tune on top with support underneath. Nearly everything else in this comparison follows from that single shift, which is why it is worth stating first rather than listing as one difference among many.

**The continuo.** Baroque ensemble music almost always has one: a bass line played by a low string instrument, with a **harpsichord** or organ realising the chords above it. Classical music has none. The usual answer is that it simply went out of fashion, but there is a musical reason. A continuo exists to supply the harmony underneath contrapuntal lines that are each busy being melodies. Once the texture is a tune over an accompaniment, the **accompaniment already is the harmony**, so a harpsichord doubling it has nothing left to do. The continuo did not fall out of favour; its job disappeared.

**Phrasing.** In counterpoint the lines overlap deliberately, each with its own shape, so the music does not fall into neat units and the ends of phrases are blurred. In melody and accompaniment the tune is in charge, and a tune comes in phrases — characteristically **four bars answered by four** in the Classical period, like a question and an answer. So balanced phrasing is not a Classical decoration; it is what happens when one line is allowed to lead.

**Cadences.** For the same reason, Classical cadences are **clear and audible** while Baroque ones are often covered by a line carrying on through them. A Classical phrase pair typically closes first on an **imperfect** cadence and then on a **perfect** one.

**Dynamics and instruments.** Baroque dynamics are **terraced** — steps between loud and soft with nothing between — because a harpsichord plucks its strings and pressing harder changes nothing. Classical dynamics are **graded**: real crescendos and diminuendos. That needed the **piano**, which strikes the strings with hammers so that touch controls volume, and a larger orchestra including **clarinets** that could swell as a body. Here the causation runs the other way: the instruments made the dynamics possible rather than the texture requiring them.

**Mood.** A Baroque movement typically holds **one mood** throughout; a Classical movement sets contrasting material against its opening, which is what makes **sonata form** possible in the first place.

**Conclusion.** The two periods differ in a long list of ways, but the list is not a list. Texture changes first; the continuo loses its function, the phrasing regularises and the cadences come into the open as consequences. Only the dynamics come from somewhere else, from what the new instruments could do. The two set works show it plainly: Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 of 1721 is contrapuntal and Beethoven's *Pathétique* of 1798 is a tune with an accompaniment, **77 years** apart.

examTechnique.body:
**Why this matters for the exam.** Area of Study 1 is **Instrumental Music 1750 to 1820**, and the two set works sit at its ends: Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 from **1721** and Beethoven's *Pathétique* from **1798**, **77 years apart**. Telling the styles apart is most of what that area of study asks.

**Get the period from the sound, then check the date.** Continuo, terraced dynamics and counterpoint mean Baroque. Melody and accompaniment, graded dynamics and a piano mean Classical or later.

**Name the period and then say why.** *Baroque* earns little. *Baroque, because a harpsichord continuo is realising the bass under the strings* earns properly.

**Remember what the instruments could do.** The harpsichord plucks, so it cannot get gradually louder. The piano hammers, so it can — and that changed how composers wrote.

**Structure changed too.** Ritornello form and ground bass belong to the Baroque; sonata form, rondo, minuet and trio and theme and variations belong to the Classical period.

**Context earns when it explains something audible.** A patron paying for music at home gets a small ensemble; a paying public in a concert hall gets an orchestra of ninety.

**Do not date music by how old it sounds.** Date it by what is playing and how the parts fit together.
examinerErrors: Using "classical" to mean all old music, when Classical with a capital C is one period of seventy years.
Naming a period without giving a single musical reason for it.
Missing the continuo, which is the fastest and most reliable clue on offer.
Calling a texture polyphonic whenever several instruments are playing, rather than when several independent melodies are.
Expecting a crescendo in Baroque music, which its keyboard instruments could not produce.
Treating the period dates as exact, and arguing with what can be heard.
Describing an orchestra as large or small without saying what is in it.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer hears the period before it thinks about dates, and gives a reason from the music every time it names one. It listens for the continuo first and knows what its absence means as well as its presence. It counts melodic lines rather than instruments, so it uses polyphony and homophony accurately. It knows why the styles changed — what the instruments could newly do, and who was paying — and it treats the boundaries as approximate, which is why it can explain a composer like Beethoven who sits across one.
